[ℱj0​𝒒−i​𝚫j+𝒒N​mj​∑ν′,𝒌′(i​𝚫j⋅ϵν′,𝒌′,j)​(𝒒⋅ϵν′,𝒌′,j∗)2​ων′,𝒌′]⋅ϵν,𝒌,j∗.\displaystyle\qquad\biggl[{\cal F}_{j}^{0}\boldsymbol{q}-i\,\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{j}+\frac{\boldsymbol{q}}{Nm_{j}}\sum_{\nu^{\prime},\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime}}\frac{(i\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{j}\cdot\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\nu^{\prime},\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime},j})(\boldsymbol{q}\cdot\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\nu^{\prime},\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime},j}^{*})}{2\omega_{\nu^{\prime},\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime}}}\biggr]\cdot\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k},j}^{*}\,.

The ll sum can be eliminated via the identity

∑lei⁡(𝒒−𝒌)⋅𝒙l=N​∑𝑮δ𝒒−𝒌,𝑮,\sum_{l}e^{i(\boldsymbol{q}-\boldsymbol{k})\cdot\boldsymbol{x}_{l}}=N\sum_{\boldsymbol{G}}\delta_{\boldsymbol{q}-\boldsymbol{k},\boldsymbol{G}}\,, (89)

where 𝒙l​j0=𝒙l+𝒙j0\boldsymbol{x}_{lj}^{0}=\boldsymbol{x}_{l}+\boldsymbol{x}_{j}^{0} with 𝒙l\boldsymbol{x}_{l} being the position of the llth primitive cell and 𝒙j0\boldsymbol{x}_{j}^{0} being the equilibrium position of the jjth atom/ion within the primitive cell, and 𝑮\boldsymbol{G} runs over the reciprocal lattice vectors. In fact, at most one term in the 𝑮\boldsymbol{G} sum is picked out for given 𝒒\boldsymbol{q} and 𝒌\boldsymbol{k}, since 𝒌∈\boldsymbol{k}\in 1BZ. We will thus drop the 𝑮\boldsymbol{G} sum in what follows. On each phonon branch, as we sum over 𝒌\boldsymbol{k}, only the mode that satisfies 𝒒=𝒌+𝑮\boldsymbol{q}=\boldsymbol{k}+\boldsymbol{G} can give a nonzero contribution to the dynamic structure factor, as a result of lattice momentum conservation.

It is worth emphasizing that the notion of momentum conservation here differs from the one familiar in particle physics, due to the spontaneous breaking of continuous translation symmetries. While each phonon can be thought of as carrying a momentum 𝒌\boldsymbol{k} within the 1BZ, it can be excited even when the momentum transfer 𝒒\boldsymbol{q} is outside the 1BZ via Umklapp scattering, in which case 𝑮≠𝟎\boldsymbol{G}\neq\boldsymbol{0}. For DM heavier than ∼\sim MeV, the momentum transfer can exceed ∼\sim keV, the typical size of the 1BZ. In this case, Umklapp processes can contribute significantly if the matrix element has support at high qq (which is the case for a heavy mediator). We will see an example of this in Sec. V.1. Note that momentum is still conserved at the fundamental level: the extra momentum 𝑮\boldsymbol{G} leads to a recoil of the entire crystal, which becomes unobservable in the limit N→∞N\to\infty. On the other hand, the notion of energy conservation is the same, as continuous time translation symmetry remains unbroken. As a result, the energy deposition has to match the phonon energy for a phonon mode to be excited.

With the equations above, we obtain the dynamic structure factor:

S⁡(𝒒,ω)\displaystyle S(\boldsymbol{q},\omega) =\displaystyle= 2​πV​∑ν∑𝒌∈1BZ|⟨ν,𝒌​|ℱT​(𝒒)|​0⟩|2​δ​(ω−ων,𝒌)\displaystyle\frac{2\pi}{V}\sum_{\nu}\sum_{\boldsymbol{k}\in\text{1BZ}}\bigl|\langle\nu,\boldsymbol{k}|{\cal F}_{T}(\boldsymbol{q})|0\rangle\bigr|^{2}\,\delta\bigl(\omega-\omega_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k}}\bigr) (90)
=\displaystyle= πΩ​∑ν1ων,𝒌​|∑je−Wj​(𝒒)mj​ei​𝑮⋅𝒙j0​(𝒀j⋅ϵν,𝒌,j∗)|2​δ​(ω−ων,𝒌),\displaystyle\frac{\pi}{\Omega}\sum_{\nu}\frac{1}{\omega_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k}}}\biggl|\sum_{j}\frac{e^{-W_{j}(\boldsymbol{q})}}{\sqrt{m_{j}}}\,e^{i\boldsymbol{G}\cdot\boldsymbol{x}_{j}^{0}}\bigl(\boldsymbol{Y}_{j}\cdot\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k},j}^{*}\bigr)\biggr|^{2}\,\delta\bigl(\omega-\omega_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k}}\bigr)\,,

where

𝒀j≡ℱj0​𝒒−i​𝚫j+Ωmj​𝒒​∑ν′∫1BZd3​k′(2​π)3​(i​𝚫j⋅ϵν′,𝒌′,j)​(𝒒⋅ϵν′,𝒌′,j∗)2​ων′,𝒌′.\boldsymbol{Y}_{j}\equiv{\cal F}_{j}^{0}\boldsymbol{q}-i\,\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{j}+\frac{\Omega}{m_{j}}\,\boldsymbol{q}\,\sum_{\nu^{\prime}}\int_{\text{1BZ}}\frac{d^{3}k^{\prime}}{(2\pi)^{3}}\,\frac{(i\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{j}\cdot\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\nu^{\prime},\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime},j})(\boldsymbol{q}\cdot\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\nu^{\prime},\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime},j}^{*})}{2\omega_{\nu^{\prime},\boldsymbol{k}^{\prime}}}\,. (91)

We have made it implicit in the last line of Eq. (90) that the 𝒌\boldsymbol{k} vector is the one inside the first Brillouin zone that satisfies 𝒒=𝒌+𝑮\boldsymbol{q}=\boldsymbol{k}+\boldsymbol{G}.

Finally, integrating over the DM velocity distribution, we obtain the rate per target mass:

R=1mcell​ρχmχ​π​σ¯2​μ2​∫d3​q(2​π)3​ℱmed2​(q)​∑ν1ων,𝒌​|∑je−Wj​(𝒒)mj​ei​𝑮⋅𝒙j0​(𝒀j⋅ϵν,𝒌,j∗)|2​g​(𝒒,ων,𝒌),R=\frac{1}{m_{\text{cell}}}\frac{\rho_{\chi}}{m_{\chi}}\frac{\pi\overline{\sigma}}{2\mu^{2}}\int\frac{d^{3}q}{(2\pi)^{3}}\,{\cal F}_{\text{med}}^{2}(q)\sum_{\nu}\frac{1}{\omega_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k}}}\,\biggl|\sum_{j}\frac{e^{-W_{j}(\boldsymbol{q})}}{\sqrt{m_{j}}}\,e^{i\boldsymbol{G}\cdot\boldsymbol{x}_{j}^{0}}\bigl(\boldsymbol{Y}_{j}\cdot\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k},j}^{*}\bigr)\biggr|^{2}\,g(\boldsymbol{q},\omega_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k}})\,, (92)

where mcell=ρT​Ωm_{\text{cell}}=\rho_{T}\Omega is the mass contained in a primitive cell. The mediator form factor ℱmed{\cal F}_{\text{med}}, the Debye-Waller factor Wj​(𝒒)W_{j}(\boldsymbol{q}) and the g⁡(𝒒,ω)g(\boldsymbol{q},\omega) function are given by Eqs. (12), (87) and (27), respectively. The DM couplings are encoded in the 𝒀j\boldsymbol{Y}_{j} vectors given in Eq. (91), with ℱj0,𝚫j{\cal F}_{j}^{0},\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{j} defined in Eq. (85). Meanwhile, the material specific quantities – phonon dispersions ων,𝒌\omega_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k}} and polarization vectors ϵν,𝒌,j\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k},j} – can be numerically computed using DFT methods detailed in our companion paper [51].

In the following subsections, we discuss the phonon excitation calculation in more detail. It is clear from the discussion above that 𝒀j\boldsymbol{Y}_{j} are the key quantities to compute for any specific DM model. In Sec. V.1, we consider the simpler case where DM couples only to nucleons but not electrons, and point out an interesting complementarity with nuclear recoils. We also discuss the relevance of Umklapp processes for DM heavier than an MeV, for both heavy and light mediators. Including DM-electron couplings introduces complications, but we show in Sec. V.2 that 𝒀j\boldsymbol{Y}_{j} take a simple form in the low qq limit for general couplings fp,n,ef_{p,n,e}. Note that the dark photon mediator benchmark (fp0=fe0,fn0=0f_{p}^{0}=f_{e}^{0},f_{n}^{0}=0) has been studied in Refs. [43, 44] based on the Fröhlich Hamiltonian. Our calculation here reproduces previous results, and helps clarify their range of validity.

V.1 Dark Matter Coupling Only to Nucleons

Setting fe=0f_{e}=0 and fψ0=fn0=fnf_{\psi}^{0}=f_{n}^{0}=f_{n} in Eq. (85), we have

ℱj0​(𝒒)=(fjfn)​FNj​(q),𝚫j​(𝒒)=𝟎.{\cal F}_{j}^{0}(\boldsymbol{q})=\biggl(\frac{f_{j}}{f_{n}}\biggr)\,F_{N_{j}}(q)\,,\qquad\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{j}(\boldsymbol{q})=\boldsymbol{0}\,. (93)

In this case, 𝒀j\boldsymbol{Y}_{j} is simply ℱj0​𝒒{\cal F}_{j}^{0}\boldsymbol{q}, and the rate Eq. (92) becomes

R\displaystyle R =\displaystyle= 1mcellρχmχπ​σ¯n2​μχ​n2∫d3​q(2​π)3ℱmed2(q)×\displaystyle\frac{1}{m_{\text{cell}}}\frac{\rho_{\chi}}{m_{\chi}}\frac{\pi\overline{\sigma}_{n}}{2\mu_{\chi n}^{2}}\int\frac{d^{3}q}{(2\pi)^{3}}\,{\cal F}_{\text{med}}^{2}(q)\times (94)
∑ν1ων,𝒌​|∑je−Wj​(𝒒)mj​fjfn​FNj​(q)​ei​𝑮⋅𝒙j0​(𝒒⋅ϵν,𝒌,j∗)|2​g​(𝒒,ων,𝒌).\displaystyle\qquad\qquad\sum_{\nu}\frac{1}{\omega_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k}}}\,\biggl|\sum_{j}\frac{e^{-W_{j}(\boldsymbol{q})}}{\sqrt{m_{j}}}\frac{f_{j}}{f_{n}}\,F_{N_{j}}(q)\,e^{i\boldsymbol{G}\cdot\boldsymbol{x}_{j}^{0}}\bigl(\boldsymbol{q}\cdot\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k},j}^{*}\bigr)\biggr|^{2}\,g(\boldsymbol{q},\omega_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k}})\,.

It is interesting to compare to the nuclear recoils case. If there is only one atom in the primitive cell, we have mcell=mj=mNm_{\text{cell}}=m_{j}=m_{N}, and

R=ρχmχ​π​σ¯n2​μχ​n2​∫d3​q(2​π)3​e−2​W​fN2fn2​FN2​ℱmed2​∑ν|𝒒⋅ϵν,𝒌∗|2mN2​ων,𝒌​g​(𝒒,ων,𝒌).R=\frac{\rho_{\chi}}{m_{\chi}}\frac{\pi\overline{\sigma}_{n}}{2\mu_{\chi n}^{2}}\int\frac{d^{3}q}{(2\pi)^{3}}\,e^{-2W}\,\frac{f_{N}^{2}}{f_{n}^{2}}F_{N}^{2}{\cal F}_{\text{med}}^{2}\sum_{\nu}\frac{\bigl|\boldsymbol{q}\cdot\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k}}^{*}\bigr|^{2}}{m_{N}^{2}\omega_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k}}}\,g(\boldsymbol{q},\omega_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k}})\,. (95)

The differential rate reads

d​Rd​ω=ρχmχ​π​σ¯n2​μχ​n2​∫d3​q(2​π)3​e−2​W​fN2fn2​FN2​ℱmed2​g​(𝒒,ω)​∑ν|𝒒⋅ϵν,𝒌∗|2mN2​ω​δ​(ω−ων,𝒌).\frac{dR}{d\omega}=\frac{\rho_{\chi}}{m_{\chi}}\frac{\pi\overline{\sigma}_{n}}{2\mu_{\chi n}^{2}}\int\frac{d^{3}q}{(2\pi)^{3}}\,e^{-2W}\,\frac{f_{N}^{2}}{f_{n}^{2}}F_{N}^{2}{\cal F}_{\text{med}}^{2}\,g(\boldsymbol{q},\omega)\sum_{\nu}\frac{\bigl|\boldsymbol{q}\cdot\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k}}^{*}\bigr|^{2}}{m_{N}^{2}\omega}\,\delta(\omega-\omega_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k}})\,.\quad (96)

On the other hand, we can rewrite Eq. (60) for nuclear recoils in terms of the g⁡(𝒒,ω)g(\boldsymbol{q},\omega) function via ∫q​𝑑q​η​(vmin)→2​∫d3​q(2​π)3​g​(𝒒,ω)\int q\,dq\,\eta(v_{\text{min}})\to 2\int\frac{d^{3}q}{(2\pi)^{3}}\,g(\boldsymbol{q},\omega), and multiply the integrand by 1=q22​mN​ω1=\frac{q^{2}}{2m_{N}\omega}:

d​Rd​ω=ρχmχ​π​σ¯n2​μχ​n2​∫d3​q(2​π)3​fN2fn2​FN2​ℱmed2​g​(𝒒,ω)​q2mN2​ω​δ​(ω−q22​mN)(nuclear recoil).\frac{dR}{d\omega}=\frac{\rho_{\chi}}{m_{\chi}}\frac{\pi\overline{\sigma}_{n}}{2\mu_{\chi n}^{2}}\int\frac{d^{3}q}{(2\pi)^{3}}\,\frac{f_{N}^{2}}{f_{n}^{2}}F_{N}^{2}{\cal F}_{\text{med}}^{2}\,g(\boldsymbol{q},\omega)\frac{q^{2}}{m_{N}^{2}\omega}\,\delta\biggl(\omega-\frac{q^{2}}{2m_{N}}\biggr)\qquad\text{(nuclear recoil)}\,. (97)

One can clearly see the similarity between Eqs. (96) and (97). However, a key difference between nuclear recoils and phonon excitations is the way in which contributions from different atoms add up in the case of more than one atoms in the primitive cell. Comparing Eq. (94) against Eq. (62), we see that, in contrast to the nuclear recoils case where we add up the rates from inequivalent nuclei, for phonon excitations the sum over jj is taken at the amplitude level. It is worth noting, however, that this apparent coherence does not result in a more favorable scaling of the detection rate. In fact, the total rate per target mass scales with neither the number of nuclei in the primitive cell, nor the total number of atoms/ions in the crystal. The former can be seen from the fact that phonon polarization vectors scale as ϵν,𝒌,j∼mj/mcell\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k},j}\sim\sqrt{m_{j}/m_{\text{cell}}}, which, together with the prefactor, means the denominator of Eq. (94) scales as mcell2m_{\text{cell}}^{2}. The latter is because of the 1/N1/\sqrt{N} normalization factor when expanding 𝒖l​j\boldsymbol{u}_{lj} in terms of phonon creation and annihilation operators (see Eq. (79)). The intuition here is that, despite the collective nature of phonon excitations, we have to project the motion of each atom onto the phonon modes that match the energy-momentum transfer. As a result, coherence between more atoms comes with a price of a smaller overlap with phonon modes.

Another key difference between nuclear recoils and phonon excitations, alluded to in Fig. 1 and Sec. III.1, is the kinematic regimes probed. In the phonon case, the Debye-Waller factor e−Wje^{-W_{j}} cuts off the momentum integral for q≳mN​ωphq\gtrsim\sqrt{m_{N}\omega_{\text{ph}}}, the inverse spatial extent of the nucleus wavefunction. The ωph\omega_{\text{ph}} here should be thought of as an average phonon energy over the entire 1BZ, which is of the same order as ωphmax\omega_{\text{ph}}^{\text{max}}. As discussed in Sec. III.1, this high qq regime is exactly where the nuclear recoil calculation becomes valid. In addition, nuclear recoils happen at much higher energy depositions ω=q2/2​mN≫ωphmax\omega=q^{2}/2m_{N}\gg\omega_{\text{ph}}^{\text{max}} than phonon excitations.

A multi-channel search can exploit this complementarity between nuclear recoils and phonon excitations. Let us consider, as a benchmark model, a hadrophilic scalar mediator coupling identically to protons and neutrons (fp=fnf_{p}=f_{n}, fe=0f_{e}=0). In Fig. 4, we compare the reach of the two channels, using GaAs as an example target material.66 6 As discussed in arXiv v3 of the companion paper [51], changes in the constraint projections via single phonon excitations in Fig. 4, relative to previous versions, are due to a bug fix in computing FNjF_{N_{j}} which altered the constraints by a factor of, approximately, 2.25. The calculations have been updated using PhonoDark v1.1.0 [67]. For a heavy mediator (left panel), we see that with sub-eV energy thresholds, nuclear recoils can probe DM masses above ∼100\sim 100\,MeV — this is the mass regime where the single phonon excitation rate suffers from Debye-Waller suppression. Below ∼100\sim 100\,MeV where nuclear recoils lose sensitivity, single phonon excitations can probe a few more orders of magnitude of mχm_{\chi}, depending on the energy threshold. For a light mediator (right panel), on the other hand, single phonon excitations outperform nuclear recoils for all mχm_{\chi}. This is because the momentum integral is dominated by the lowest qq, which only depends on the energy threshold, qmin≃ωmin/vmaxq_{\text{min}}\simeq\omega_{\text{min}}/v_{\text{max}}. The mass scaling of the curves in Fig. 4 can be understood with a close examination of phase space integrals; we reserve a detailed discussion, including how the various features of the curves depend on material properties, for the companion paper [51].

It is also worth noting that while direct production of single phonons has been proposed mainly as a channel to search for sub-MeV DM, we see from Fig. 4 that its sensitivity extends well above MeV DM masses, which is important for covering the parameter space out of reach in nuclear recoils. A DM particle heavier than ∼\sim MeV carries a momentum larger than the typical size of the 1BZ (or equivalently, the inverse lattice spacing). However, as explained below Eq. (89), a crystal target is able to absorb a momentum transfer beyond the 1BZ while still producing a phonon, provided the energy deposition matches that of the phonon energy. Such Umklapp processes can contribute significantly to the rate. In Fig. 5, we examine the role of Umklapp scattering by comparing the full rate (solid) vs. contributions from q∈q\in 1BZ (dashed), for three DM masses. We show the differential distribution up to 34 meV, the highest phonon energy in GaAs. For mχ=0.1m_{\chi}=0.1\,MeV, the maximum momentum transfer qmax≃2​mχ​vmax≃0.56​keVq_{\text{max}}\simeq 2m_{\chi}v_{\text{max}}\simeq 0.56\,\text{keV} is within the 1BZ, so the solid and dashed histograms coincide. Also, only acoustic phonons with energies below cs​qmax≃9c_{s}q_{\text{max}}\simeq 9\,meV (where csc_{s} is the speed of sound) and optical phonons are kinematically accessible; contributions from optical phonons are suppressed at low qq [69], so the total rate is dominated by the low energy acoustic phonons. For mχ=1m_{\chi}=1\,MeV and 10 MeV, Umklapp processes dominate the rate in the heavy mediator case, since the momentum integral is dominated by large qq. In the light mediator case, the matrix element peaks at small qq, so the total rate is well approximated by the 1BZ contribution for sufficiently low energy thresholds (e.g. 1 meV). However, Umklapp scattering can still contribute significantly in the highest energy bins, and dominate the rate if the energy threshold is higher (e.g. 30 meV).

V.2 Dark Matter With Couplings to Electrons

In the presence of electron couplings fe≠0f_{e}\neq 0, information about electron distributions is needed for the rate calculation. We focus on ionic crystals in this subsection, for which Eq. (82) is a good approximation, and the rate formula Eq. (92) directly applies. In this case, we need n~ej\widetilde{n}_{e}^{j} and δ​n~el​j/δ​𝒖l​j\delta\widetilde{n}_{e}^{lj}/\delta\boldsymbol{u}_{lj} as input. While n~ej\widetilde{n}_{e}^{j} can be derived from the same electron wavefunctions as those used in electron transition calculations in Sec. IV, δ​n~el​j/δ​𝒖l​j\delta\widetilde{n}_{e}^{lj}/\delta\boldsymbol{u}_{lj} is challenging to compute numerically for general 𝒒\boldsymbol{q} and 𝒖l​j\boldsymbol{u}_{lj}.

However, the calculation simplifies in the limit q≪rion−1q\ll r_{\text{ion}}^{-1}, the inverse ionic radii. As in classical electromagnetism, we can make a multipole expansion,

n~ej​(−𝒒)=∫Ωl​jd3​r​ei​𝒒⋅𝒓​nel​j​(𝒓)=Ne,j−i​𝒒⋅𝑷e,j+𝒪⁡(q2),\widetilde{n}_{e}^{j}(-\boldsymbol{q})=\int_{\Omega_{lj}}d^{3}r\,e^{i\boldsymbol{q}\cdot\boldsymbol{r}}n_{e}^{lj}(\boldsymbol{r})=N_{e,j}-i\boldsymbol{q}\cdot\boldsymbol{P}_{e,j}+\mathcal{O}(q^{2})\,, (98)

where Ne,jN_{e,j} is the number of electrons associated with site l,jl,j, and 𝑷e,j\boldsymbol{P}_{e,j} is the electron contribution to the polarization in the volume Ωl​j\Omega_{lj}. Consider the response of the total polarization of the volume to a lattice displacement 𝒖l​j\boldsymbol{u}_{lj}:

δ​𝑷l​j=Qj​δ​𝒖l​j+δ​𝑷e,j,\delta\boldsymbol{P}_{lj}=Q_{j}\,\delta\boldsymbol{u}_{lj}+\delta\boldsymbol{P}_{e,j}\,, (99)

where Qj=Zj−Ne,jQ_{j}=Z_{j}-N_{e,j} is the total charge. This defines the Born effective charge tensor:77 7 More precisely, the Born effective charge 𝒁j∗\boldsymbol{Z}^{*}_{j} is defined as the change in macroscopic polarization caused by a uniform displacement of the entire sublattice jj [70]. However, under the assumption we have made in Eq. (82) – that the electrons respond locally to the ionic displacements – the precise definition is equivalent to Eq. (100).

𝒁j∗≡δ​𝑷l​jδ​𝒖l​j=Qj​𝟙+δ​𝑷e,jδ​𝒖l​j.\boldsymbol{Z}_{j}^{*}\equiv\frac{\delta\boldsymbol{P}_{lj}}{\delta\boldsymbol{u}_{lj}}=Q_{j}\mathbbm{1}+\frac{\delta\boldsymbol{P}_{e,j}}{\delta\boldsymbol{u}_{lj}}\,. (100)

Thus,

δ​n~el​j​(−𝒒)δ​𝒖l​j=−i𝒒⋅δ​𝑷e,jδ​𝒖l​j+𝒪(q2)=−i𝒒⋅(𝒁j∗−Qj𝟙)+𝒪(q2).\frac{\delta\widetilde{n}_{e}^{lj}(-\boldsymbol{q})}{\delta\boldsymbol{u}_{lj}}=-i\boldsymbol{q}\cdot\frac{\delta\boldsymbol{P}_{e,j}}{\delta\boldsymbol{u}_{lj}}+\mathcal{O}(q^{2})=-i\boldsymbol{q}\cdot(\boldsymbol{Z}_{j}^{*}-Q_{j}\mathbbm{1})+\mathcal{O}(q^{2})\,. (101)

From Eqs. (98) and (101), we obtain (choosing f0=fe0f^{0}=f_{e}^{0} in the normalization):

ℱj0​(𝒒)\displaystyle{\cal F}_{j}^{0}(\boldsymbol{q}) =\displaystyle= fpfe0​Zj+fnfe0​(Aj−Zj)+fefe0​Ne,j+𝒪⁡(q),\displaystyle\frac{f_{p}}{f_{e}^{0}}Z_{j}+\frac{f_{n}}{f_{e}^{0}}(A_{j}-Z_{j})+\frac{f_{e}}{f_{e}^{0}}N_{e,j}+\mathcal{O}(q)\,, (102)
𝚫j​(𝒒)\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{j}(\boldsymbol{q}) =\displaystyle= −fefe0i𝒒⋅(𝒁j∗−Qj𝟙)+𝒪(q2),\displaystyle-\frac{f_{e}}{f_{e}^{0}}\,i\boldsymbol{q}\cdot(\boldsymbol{Z}_{j}^{*}-Q_{j}\mathbbm{1})+\mathcal{O}(q^{2})\,, (103)

where we have set FN,j​(𝒒)=1F_{N,j}(\boldsymbol{q})=1 since q≪rion−1q\ll r_{\text{ion}}^{-1} is much smaller than the inverse nucleus radius. We therefore obtain the following simple expression for 𝒀j\boldsymbol{Y}_{j}:

𝒀j=𝒒⋅[fpfe0​Zj​ 1+fnfe0​(Aj−Zj)​ 1+fefe0​(Zj​𝟙−𝒁j∗)]+𝒪⁡(q2).\boldsymbol{Y}_{j}=\boldsymbol{q}\cdot\biggl[\frac{f_{p}}{f_{e}^{0}}Z_{j}\,\mathbbm{1}+\frac{f_{n}}{f_{e}^{0}}(A_{j}-Z_{j})\,\mathbbm{1}+\frac{f_{e}}{f_{e}^{0}}(Z_{j}\mathbbm{1}-\boldsymbol{Z}_{j}^{*})\biggr]+\mathcal{O}(q^{2})\,. (104)

In the case of a vector or scalar mediator, the coupling ratios appearing in Eq. (104) should incorporate in-medium screening effects according to Eq. (50). As mentioned at the beginning of Sec. II.2, while dielectric response of an ionic crystal comes from both electrons and ions at phonon frequencies, only the electron contribution is included in the derivation of Eq. (50). That this is the correct treatment should be clear from the calculation above. Polarization induced by lattice displacements has been treated as an effective charge density ∇⋅𝑷\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol{P}, since it can induce the transition |0⟩→|ν,𝒌⟩|0\rangle\to|\nu,\boldsymbol{k}\rangle. As such, it enters the source term rather than the dielectric matrix 𝜺\boldsymbol{\varepsilon} in Maxwell’s equations. In the low qq limit, electron contributions to 𝜺\boldsymbol{\varepsilon} below the electronic band gap approach a constant 𝜺∞\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{\infty}, referred to as the high-frequency dielectric constant.

In the special case of a dark photon mediator that kinetically mixes with the SM photon, fp0=−fe0f_{p}^{0}=-f_{e}^{0}, fn0=0f_{n}^{0}=0. Combining Eqs. (104) and (50), and setting 𝜺→𝜺∞\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\to\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{\infty}, we obtain

𝒀j=−q2𝒒⋅𝜺∞⋅𝒒​(𝒒⋅𝒁j∗).\boldsymbol{Y}_{j}=-\frac{q^{2}}{\boldsymbol{q}\cdot\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{\infty}\cdot\boldsymbol{q}}(\boldsymbol{q}\cdot\boldsymbol{Z}_{j}^{*})\,. (105)

By Eq. (92), the rate is therefore

R\displaystyle R =\displaystyle= 1mcellρχmχπ​σ¯e2​μχ​e2∫d3​q(2​π)3ℱmed2(q)q4(𝒒⋅𝜺∞⋅𝒒)2×\displaystyle\frac{1}{m_{\text{cell}}}\frac{\rho_{\chi}}{m_{\chi}}\frac{\pi\overline{\sigma}_{e}}{2\mu_{\chi e}^{2}}\int\frac{d^{3}q}{(2\pi)^{3}}\,{\cal F}_{\text{med}}^{2}(q)\,\frac{q^{4}}{(\boldsymbol{q}\cdot\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{\infty}\cdot\boldsymbol{q})^{2}}\times (106)
∑ν1ων,𝒌​|∑je−Wj​(𝒒)mj​ei​𝑮⋅𝒙j0​(𝒒⋅𝒁j∗⋅ϵν,𝒌,j∗)|2​g​(𝒒,ων,𝒌).\displaystyle\qquad\qquad\sum_{\nu}\frac{1}{\omega_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k}}}\,\biggl|\sum_{j}\frac{e^{-W_{j}(\boldsymbol{q})}}{\sqrt{m_{j}}}\,e^{i\boldsymbol{G}\cdot\boldsymbol{x}_{j}^{0}}\bigl(\boldsymbol{q}\cdot\boldsymbol{Z}_{j}^{*}\cdot\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k},j}^{*}\bigr)\biggr|^{2}\,g(\boldsymbol{q},\omega_{\nu,\boldsymbol{k}})\,.

Note that since Eq. (104) for 𝒀j\boldsymbol{Y}_{j} is derived in the limit q≪rion−1∼𝒪⁡(keV)q\ll r_{\text{ion}}^{-1}\sim\mathcal{O}(\text{keV}), Eq. (106) holds only when the integral is dominated by this region. This is the case for a light dark photon mediator for any DM mass, since the integrand peaks at small qq. In this case, Eq. (106) is in agreement with the result obtain in Ref. [44] based on the Fröhlich Hamiltonian. For a heavy mediator, on the other hand, the integrand peaks at qmax=2​mχ​vmaxq_{\text{max}}=2m_{\chi}v_{\text{max}}, so Eq. (106) holds only for mχ≪(2​vmax​rion)−1∼𝒪⁡(MeV)m_{\chi}\ll(2v_{\text{max}}r_{\text{ion}})^{-1}\sim\mathcal{O}(\text{MeV}).

Beyond the previously studied dark photon mediator case, our first-principle rate derivation here allows us to compute the reach for other DM models with couplings to electrons. As examples, we consider two benchmark models from Ref. [62] – a hadrophobic light scalar mediator and a light U​(1)B−LU(1)_{B-L} vector mediator. In both cases, astrophysical constraints already rule out all of the parameter space within reach of proposed experiments if χ\chi composes all the DM. We find similar results here: for a hadrophobic light scalar mediator, the astrophysical constraints extend past the reach of single phonon excitations in a GaAs target; for a light U​(1)B−LU(1)_{B-L} vector mediator, for mχ≳100m_{\chi}\gtrsim 100 MeV and ωmin=1\omega_{\text{min}}=1 meV, the reach extends slightly past the astrophysical constraints, but the rest of the parameter space is constrained. Therefore, as in Ref. [62], we consider the case where χ\chi is a 5% subcomponent of DM, in which case SIDM constraints are absent and single phonon excitations can probe currently unconstrained parameter space. The projected reach for both benchmark models is shown in Fig. 6, where a mediator mass of 1 eV is assumed for definiteness.88 8 Changes in the single phonon excitation reach in the left panel of Fig. 6, relative to previous versions, are due to the inclusion of screening effects in DM models coupling to the electron number density via a scalar mediator. The calculations have been updated using PhonoDark v1.1.0 [67].

VI Conclusions

Dark matter direct detection has entered an era in which not only the mass coverage is extending beyond the classic WIMP window – especially into the sub-GeV regime – but also multi-channel target response is becoming an important consideration when designing new experiments. In this paper, we detailed a theoretical framework for calculating spin-independent direct detection rates that can be applied across multiple search channels. Starting from generic DM couplings to the proton, neutron and electron, we factored out material and channel dependent target response into the dynamic structure factor, and derived a procedure to compute this factor which involves quantizing number density operators in the appropriate Hilbert space. We focused on 𝒪⁡(eV)\mathcal{O}(\text{eV})-gap crystal targets where existing and proposed search channels include nuclear recoils, electron transitions and single phonon excitations, each probing a different kinematic regime (see Fig. 1). Despite the apparently very different physics involved, the calculation proceeds analogously for all three channels.

While part of this paper has been devoted to rederiving known results in this unified framework, we also obtained several new results, which we summarize in the following:

  • •

    We have clarified the range of validity of the standard nuclear recoils calculation (Sec. III.1). For energy depositions lower than 𝒪⁡(100​meV)\mathcal{O}(100\,\text{meV}) in a crystal target, the picture of scattering off single nuclei breaks down. Collective motions of all nuclei have to be considered, with phonons being the appropriate degrees of freedom. The situation is analogous in fluids, though the energy cutoff can be lower (e.g. 𝒪⁡(meV)\mathcal{O}(\text{meV}) for superfluid helium).

  • •

    We have extended the electron transition calculation to account for anisotropic target response, and pointed out the resulting daily modulation can be significant (Sec. IV.1). As an example, we considered hexagonal boron nitride, a semiconductor with a 6 eV gap and layered crystal structure, and showed that ±(10​-​ 40)%\pm(10\,\text{-}\,40)\% daily modulation can be expected, depending on the DM mass (Fig. 3).

  • •

    As a major new result, we have presented a first-principle derivation of single phonon excitation rates for generic SI couplings. The final result is Eq. (92), where dependence on the relative couplings to the proton, neutron, and electron is fully captured by the quantities 𝒀j\boldsymbol{Y}_{j}. Computing 𝒀j\boldsymbol{Y}_{j} is straightforward for DM coupling only to nucleons (Sec. V.1), but nontrivial in the presence of coupling to electrons (Sec. V.2). In the latter case, we have shown that 𝒀j\boldsymbol{Y}_{j} are related to the Born effective charges in an ionic crystal for a general light mediator (not necessarily a dark photon) – see Eq. (104). As examples, we computed the reach for DM scattering via a light hadrophobic scalar or U​(1)B−LU(1)_{B-L} vector mediator (Fig. 6), where single phonon excitations offer a complementary search channel with competitive sensitivities to previous proposals [62].

  • •

    We have pointed out that sensitivity of the single phonon excitation channel is not restricted to sub-MeV DM. For heavier DM, Umklapp contribution can be significant (Fig. 5), and single phonon excitations and nuclear recoils play complementary roles in probing the DM parameter space (Fig. 4).

In addition to shedding light on the connection and complementarity between various existing and proposed direct detection channels, the theoretical framework presented here also makes clear that there is a common algorithm one can follow to study yet unexplored novel detection channels in the future. Some of them will require extending our present formalism beyond SI interactions, a task we plan to take on in future work.

Appendix A DFT Calculation Details for BN

We used the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP) [72, 73, 74, 75] for our density functional theory calculations to obtain the electronic properties of BN. Projector augmented wave (PAW) pseudopotentials [76, 77] with the Perdew-Becke-Ernzerhof (PBE) exchange-correlation functional [78] were used. We included van der Waals interactions between BN layers using the D3 correction method of Grimme et al. with Becke-Johnson damping [79, 80]. In the PAW scheme, we treated s and p electrons as valence for both B and N.

For structural optimization, we use an energy cutoff of 950 eV for our plane wave basis set, with a Gamma-centered k-point grid of 12×12×1212\times 12\times 12. The total energy and forces were converged to 1×1081\times 10^{8} eV and 1 meV/Å respectively. Wavefunctions were evaluated on two Gamma-centered k-point meshes, 10×10×310\times 10\times 3, and 14×14×414\times 14\times 4, converging the scattering rate to ∼9%\sim 9\% at 5 MeV, ∼8%\sim 8\% at 10 MeV and ∼6%\sim 6\% at 100 MeV. We extracted the all-electron wavefunction coefficients from our PAW calculations using pawpyseed [81] with an energy cutoff of 450 eV. 68 energy bands were included, incorporating energies up to 60 eV above and below the valence band maximum.

Boron nitride (BN) adopts a hexagonal crystal structure with space group P​63/m​m​cP6_{3}/mmc (No. 194) as shown in Fig. 2. Our calculated lattice parameters are a=2.507a=2.507 Å and c=7.093c=7.093 Å  which compare well to those from experiment [82] (a=2.504a=2.504 Å and c=6.661c=6.661 Å). The PBE-level calculated band gap is 3.61 eV which was corrected to the experimental value of 5.97 eV [83] using a scissors operator.
